title: The Tie That Holds
endLine: The plateau lasts while small inward and outward currents nearly cancel.

scenes.tts: A nerve spike is over almost at once. Excite a ventricular heart cell, and it stays depolarized roughly a hundred times as long. What holds it up there?
scenes.narration: A nerve spike is over almost at once. Excite a ventricular heart cell, and it stays depolarized roughly a hundred times as long. What holds it up there?
scenes.caption: A nerve spike is over almost at once. Excite a ventricular heart cell, and it stays depolarized roughly a hundred times as long. What holds it up there?
scenes.visual: THE WORLD, built here and kept for the whole film (16:9). COLOUR BY CONCEPT, same in every scene: voltage trace bright WHITE; sodium CORAL dots; calcium GOLD dots; potassium BLUE dots; cell interior pale grey. Layout: LEFT 60% of the frame is one large voltage-against-time plot, y axis -90 to +40 mV, x axis 0 to 400 ms. RIGHT 40% is a tall slice of one cell's membrane, outside at the right, inside at the left, with empty channel slots. A small tag 'schematic, teaching values' stays at bottom left all film. Hook motion: a thin spike 3 ms wide, labelled 'nerve spike', flicks up and down at the left of the plot. Then a WHITE dot draws the ventricular trace across the same axis, 300 ms wide (100 times the spike), labelled 'ventricular cell'. On the question the dot stops high on the trace and white text appears: 'What holds it up?'

Title 'The Tie That Holds' fades in above the plot for 2 s. The ventricular trace rewinds smoothly to a flat line at -90 mV; the nerve spike fades away for good. Faint dots drift on both sides of the membrane.

scenes.tts: Picture one ventricular cell from a human heart. At rest its voltage sits flat, near minus ninety millivolts. A potassium current called I K one holds it there.
scenes.narration: Picture one ventricular cell from a human heart. At rest its voltage sits flat, near minus ninety millivolts. A potassium current called IK1 holds it there.
scenes.caption: Picture one ventricular cell from a human heart. At rest its voltage sits flat, near minus ninety millivolts. A potassium current called IK1 holds it there.
scenes.visual: The WHITE dot rests on the flat line at -90 mV, with a gentle pulse. On 'I K one' a wide BLUE door opens in the membrane slice, labelled 'IK1', and BLUE dots flicker through it in both directions with a slight net outward drift. A dashed line at -90 mV is labelled 'rest'.

scenes.tts: Now sodium channels open, and the voltage shoots up past zero. Those channels inactivate within milliseconds, and a brief outward potassium current cuts a small notch.
scenes.narration: Now sodium channels open, and the voltage shoots up past zero. Those channels inactivate within milliseconds, and a brief outward potassium current cuts a small notch.
scenes.caption: Now sodium channels open, and the voltage shoots up past zero. Those channels inactivate within milliseconds, and a brief outward potassium current cuts a small notch.
scenes.visual: A CORAL channel opens in the membrane; a burst of CORAL dots rushes inward. The WHITE dot climbs steeply from -90 to about +30 mV, drawing the upstroke. On 'inactivate' the CORAL channel snaps shut with a small bar across it and stays shut all film. A narrow BLUE gate blinks open, a few BLUE dots leave, and the trace dips to about +5 mV to draw the notch. As the voltage rises, the wide IK1 door swings almost shut and fades back out of attention: IK1 is largely shut from here until repolarization.
No narration; motion continues. The WHITE dot rides slowly over the notch while the barred CORAL channel dims and faint dots drift on both sides of the membrane.

scenes.tts: Yet the voltage does not fall back. It hangs near zero for about two hundred milliseconds. This long stretch is the plateau.
scenes.narration: Yet the voltage does not fall back. It hangs near zero for about two hundred milliseconds. This long stretch is the plateau.
scenes.caption: Yet the voltage does not fall back. It hangs near zero for about two hundred milliseconds. This long stretch is the plateau.
scenes.visual: The WHITE dot moves right almost level, near 0 mV. A bracket grows under the trace as it goes, reaching 200 ms on the x axis, labelled 'plateau, about 200 ms'. The barred CORAL channel pulses once to show it is not the cause. The IK1 door stays nearly shut and dim throughout the plateau.

scenes.tts: Two sets of channels pull against each other. L type calcium channels let calcium flow in. Delayed rectifier potassium channels let potassium flow out.
scenes.narration: Two sets of channels pull against each other. L-type calcium channels let calcium flow in. Delayed-rectifier potassium channels let potassium flow out.
scenes.caption: Two sets of channels pull against each other. L-type calcium channels let calcium flow in. Delayed-rectifier potassium channels let potassium flow out.
scenes.visual: Rewind the dot to the start of the plateau. A GOLD channel labelled 'L-type calcium' opens and a steady stream of GOLD dots flows inward. A BLUE channel labelled 'IKr and IKs' opens and a matching stream of BLUE dots flows outward. Two thick arrows grow at the membrane, GOLD pointing in and BLUE pointing out, almost equal in length.
No narration; motion continues. GOLD dots stream in and BLUE dots stream out at matching rates while the two arrows hold almost equal length.

scenes.tts: Here is the one idea. The plateau is a near tie. Inward and outward currents almost cancel, so the voltage changes only slowly, drifting down as the outward currents gain.
scenes.narration: Here is the one idea. The plateau is a near tie. Inward and outward currents almost cancel, so the voltage changes only slowly, drifting down as the outward currents gain.
scenes.caption: Here is the one idea. The plateau is a near tie. Inward and outward currents almost cancel, so the voltage changes only slowly, drifting down as the outward currents gain.
scenes.visual: The two arrows slide together into a tug-of-war rope across the membrane, with a marker at its centre. Large white text: 'A near tie'. As the WHITE dot creeps along the plateau, the BLUE arrow lengthens very slightly, the marker edges toward BLUE, and the trace slopes gently downward from about +10 to 0 mV.
No narration; motion continues. GOLD dots stream in, BLUE dots stream out, the rope marker trembles near its centre, and the WHITE dot keeps creeping along the plateau.

scenes.tts: But at rest, a large potassium conductance held this cell near minus ninety. Why doesn't it drag the voltage straight back down?
scenes.narration: But at rest, a large potassium conductance held this cell near minus ninety. Why doesn't it drag the voltage straight back down?
scenes.caption: But at rest, a large potassium conductance held this cell near minus ninety. Why doesn't it drag the voltage straight back down?
scenes.visual: The nearly shut IK1 door stays dim. Beside it a dashed GHOST outline of the wide door from rest appears, labelled 'at rest', to recall the large resting conductance. A ghost dashed WHITE line drops from the plateau straight down to -90 mV, showing the fall that does not happen. White question mark beside the door. GOLD and BLUE streams continue.

scenes.tts: Because I K one is an inward rectifier. It passes current well near rest, but largely shuts at plateau voltages. So total conductance is low, and small currents hold the voltage.
scenes.narration: Because IK1 is an inward rectifier. It passes current well near rest, but largely shuts at plateau voltages. So total conductance is low, and small currents hold the voltage.
scenes.caption: Because IK1 is an inward rectifier. It passes current well near rest, but largely shuts at plateau voltages. So total conductance is low, and small currents hold the voltage.
scenes.visual: The ghost line and the dashed wide-door outline fade, leaving the real IK1 door nearly closed with a thin crack, now lit and labelled 'IK1 largely shut'. The GOLD and BLUE streams thin to a few dots each, still nearly equal, and the rope stays centred. Small label: 'small currents'.
No narration; motion continues. The thin GOLD and BLUE streams keep crossing, the IK1 door stays nearly shut, and the WHITE dot creeps along the plateau.

scenes.tts: So this balance is easy to disturb. Block just one of the outward potassium currents. What happens to the plateau?
scenes.narration: So this balance is easy to disturb. Block just one of the outward potassium currents. What happens to the plateau?
scenes.caption: So this balance is easy to disturb. Block just one of the outward potassium currents. What happens to the plateau?
scenes.visual: A white bar slides across part of the BLUE 'IKr and IKs' channel and the BLUE stream thins. The trace rewinds to the start of the plateau and the current plateau bracket stays visible. Question card across the top in white: 'Block one outward current: the plateau?'
Predict pause. The question card stays. Near-stillness by design: the rope marker trembles, a few dots bob at the membrane, the WHITE dot waits at the start of the plateau. Do not show the outcome.

scenes.tts: It lengthens. Drugs that block the potassium channel called h E R G do this. The longer plateau reaches the skin too, as a longer Q T interval on the E C G.
scenes.narration: It lengthens. Drugs that block the potassium channel called hERG do this. The longer plateau reaches the skin too, as a longer QT interval on the ECG.
scenes.caption: It lengthens. Drugs that block the potassium channel called hERG do this. The longer plateau reaches the skin too, as a longer QT interval on the ECG.
scenes.visual: The question card dissolves. The WHITE dot runs on along the plateau and past the end of the original bracket; the original trace stays as a faint ghost so the extension is visible (extension schematic, no number). The partly barred BLUE channel gets the label 'hERG'. A small strip at the bottom of the plot shows two plain bars, 'QT' and a longer 'QT'.
No narration; motion continues. The WHITE dot finishes the longer plateau beside the faint original trace, and the longer QT bar settles into place.

scenes.tts: Losing one current is partly covered, though. Several potassium currents can repolarize the cell. That margin is called the repolarization reserve.
scenes.narration: Losing one current is partly covered, though. Several potassium currents can repolarize the cell. That margin is called the repolarization reserve.
scenes.caption: Losing one current is partly covered, though. Several potassium currents can repolarize the cell. That margin is called the repolarization reserve.
scenes.visual: The bar lifts from the channel and the trace returns to its original shape. Three BLUE channels pulse in turn; one dims, and the other two brighten to take up part of its stream. Label: 'repolarization reserve'.

scenes.tts: How does the tie finally break? The L type channels inactivate, shutting with time at depolarized voltages, and as calcium builds up inside. Calcium's pull fades, and the potassium currents win.
scenes.narration: How does the tie finally break? The L-type channels inactivate, shutting with time at depolarized voltages, and as calcium builds up inside. Calcium's pull fades, and the potassium currents win.
scenes.caption: How does the tie finally break? The L-type channels inactivate, shutting with time at depolarized voltages, and as calcium builds up inside. Calcium's pull fades, and the potassium currents win.
scenes.visual: GOLD dots gather just inside the membrane. The GOLD channel slowly closes and its stream thins to nothing. The GOLD arrow shrinks, the BLUE arrow wins, and the rope marker slides fully to the BLUE side. The WHITE dot leaves the plateau and starts to fall.

scenes.tts: As the voltage falls, I K one conducts again and finishes repolarization. The cell returns to where it started, flat near minus ninety millivolts.
scenes.narration: As the voltage falls, IK1 conducts again and finishes repolarization. The cell returns to where it started, flat near minus ninety millivolts.
scenes.caption: As the voltage falls, IK1 conducts again and finishes repolarization. The cell returns to where it started, flat near minus ninety millivolts.
scenes.visual: The IK1 door swings wide open again as the WHITE dot falls faster, reaching -90 mV at about 320 ms on the x axis. The complete trace now stands on the plot, from rest through upstroke, notch, plateau and fall, and the dot settles on the dashed 'rest' line.
No narration; motion continues. The WHITE dot rests on the dashed rest line, the complete trace glows along its length, and BLUE dots flicker through the open IK1 door.

scenes.tts: So the long hold takes no huge current. It takes opposing pulls, closely matched, while the resting potassium path is largely shut. When the match ends, the plateau ends.
scenes.narration: So the long hold takes no huge current. It takes opposing pulls, closely matched, while the resting potassium path is largely shut. When the match ends, the plateau ends.
scenes.caption: So the long hold takes no huge current. It takes opposing pulls, closely matched, while the resting potassium path is largely shut. When the match ends, the plateau ends.
scenes.visual: The trace replays quickly once. Along the plateau the GOLD and BLUE arrows return, nearly equal, with the IK1 door nearly closed. At the end of the plateau the arrows part and the trace falls. The plateau section of the trace stays lit.

End card over the dimmed world, large white text, centred: 'The plateau lasts while small inward and outward currents nearly cancel.' GOLD and BLUE dots still drift slowly across the membrane behind it.
